questions.learningObjective: Determine output per worker from two plants' output and headcount
questions.stem: A transit board compares two bus overhaul shops. One employs 40 workers and rebuilds 8 vehicles a month; the other employs 25 workers and rebuilds 10. What does the comparison show?

options.text: The second shop produces more per worker, so its labor is used more productively
The first shop is more productive because it employs more people on its payroll
options.misconception: Confuses total headcount with output per worker

options.text: The comparison proves nothing, because the two shops rebuild different kinds of vehicle

options.text: Payroll size is the most reliable measure of how efficiently a shop actually works
options.misconception: Treats payroll size as the measure of efficiency

questions.explanation: Output per worker is units divided by workers, so 8 over 40 is 0.20 vehicles against 10 over 25 at 0.40. The second shop produces twice as much per worker, so it uses labor more productively.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single demand-side lever fails under stagflation
questions.stem: A transit board's economist explains why a council facing both rising prices and rising joblessness cannot simply ask the central bank to make things easier. Explain the reasoning fully.

answer.exemplar: When prices and unemployment rise together, the usual demand-side remedy backfires: easier money stimulates spending, which pushes inflation higher without drawing idle workers back into jobs. Policymakers must instead weigh supply-side measures, which fight inflation slowly, against tolerating weaker output, which is politically costly but may reduce price pressure.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains why a single demand-side lever cannot fix both problems and identifies what the board can actually control. It should also acknowledge the cost of each available option rather than promise a painless choice.
questions.hint: Ask why one familiar remedy backfires here.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how labor productivity can rise without new capital equipment
questions.stem: A transit board asks why output per worker can rise even when a plant adds no new machines. Explain the mechanism clearly.

answer.exemplar: Output per worker rises when the same labor produces more output, and that can come from better organization, a change in product mix, less time lost to setup and rework, or a shift toward tasks that are faster to complete. Capital is one way to raise productivity, but rearranging how existing labor and equipment are used can do the same job without any new machine being bought.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies at least two organizational routes to higher output per worker and rules out the assumption that machines are required. It should also avoid confusing higher output with higher value added per worker.
questions.hint: Name one way to change output without new hardware.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how assembly-line production reshaped factory skill requirements
questions.stem: A transit board's trainer asks you to explain how assembly-line production changed the skill profile of factory work. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Assembly-line production divided a job into narrow, repeatable steps, so a plant could hire many workers with limited factory experience and train them quickly on a single task. Skill became less about knowing how to build the whole product and more about doing one step consistently, which changed both the labor market the plant drew from and the bargaining position of the workers inside it.

questions.explanation: A strong answer connects the division of labor to the reduced skill needed per worker, and then to the wider labor market effects. It should avoid claiming the work became skill-free, which overstates the case.
questions.hint: Ask what a new hire must know to be useful.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how capital borrowing can weaken operating budgets
questions.stem: A transit board asks an aide to describe how a city in long decline handles a bond issue that voters approved for capital work. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: When voters approve a capital bond, the city gains money for construction but must still repay it with interest from future budgets, and that repayment competes with operating costs. questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that capital borrowing creates future repayment obligations rather than free money. It should note that improvements can look like progress while quietly crowding out the operating budget.

questions.stem: A council aide asks you to explain why a period of rising prices and rising unemployment is harder for a transit board to plan for than either trend alone. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: Rising prices alone push up the cost of every contract the board signs, while rising joblessness alone makes the ridership forecast uncertain. answer.exemplar: Output per worker measures how much a plant produces for each person it employs, so it rises when the plant gets more out of the same crew or hires fewer people for the same output. questions.learningObjective: Explain how a moving line reshapes quality control in a repair shop
questions.stem: A transit board asks you to explain how a moving assembly line changes quality control in a bus repair shop. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: A moving line fixes the sequence of steps and the pace at which each is performed, which reduces variation between workers and makes a fault less likely to slip past in one station than the next. questions.explanation: A strong answer connects the fixed sequence to fewer variations and lower defect rates, then notes the new risk of a repeated systematic error. It should avoid claiming the line removes the need for inspection.

options.text: Scarcity means the tax rate should be set by the highest bidder for the site
options.misconception: Confuses a property decision with a revenue auction

options.text: Scarcity means the board can demand any price, since the land has no alternative use
options.misconception: Assumes scarcity gives the city unlimited bargaining power

options.text: Scarcity means the plant should be allowed to close, since the site is too valuable to keep
options.misconception: Assumes scarcity argues for abandoning industrial use

options.text: The site's scarcity raises its value to future users, so any offer should be judged against that scarcity

questions.explanation: Scarcity raises the value of the site and the cost of letting it idle, so the board should weigh the opportunity cost of losing it. It does not give unlimited power, nor argue for closure.
questions.hint: Ask what the district gives up if the site sits empty.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a percentage gain in output per worker
questions.stem: A board study compares a shop before and after standardization. Output per worker rises from 2.4 to 3.1 units an hour. What was the approximate percentage gain?

options.text: About 23 percent, since 0.7 divided by 3.1 gives roughly 0.23 of the new rate
options.misconception: Divides by the new figure and misreads the result

options.text: About 29 percent, since 0.7 divided by 2.4 is roughly 0.29
About 70 percent, since the change amounted to 0.7 units an hour
options.misconception: Confuses the absolute change with the percentage gain

options.text: About 3 percent, since the difference was 0.7 units an hour
options.misconception: Confuses a unit change with a percentage change

questions.explanation: The gain is 3.1 minus 2.4, which is 0.7 units an hour, and 0.7 over the original 2.4 is about 0.29. The denominator is the starting value, which is what makes it a percentage change.
questions.hint: Divide the change by the original rate of 2.4.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a regional report on industrial decline and its uneven effects

stimulus.body: The review finds that between 1960 and 1980 the region's plant count fell by 60 percent, that output per remaining worker rose by 40 percent, and that average wages there grew more slowly than in the country as a whole. It notes that two counties with diversified economies gained employment.

questions.stem: According to the review, which combination best characterizes the region's industrial change?

options.text: The same number of plants, since a 40 percent productivity rise offsets the closures
options.misconception: Treats productivity gains as restoring plant numbers

options.text: Fewer plants but more workers, since output per worker rose by 40 percent
options.misconception: Assumes higher output per worker means more workers

options.text: Fewer plants and fewer workers, with higher output per remaining worker and slower wage growth
Fewer plants and faster wage growth, because output per worker rose in the region
options.misconception: Reverses the report's statement about wages

questions.explanation: The review pairs a 60 percent plant loss with a 40 percent rise in output per remaining worker, which means employment also fell while wages lagged nationally. Diversified counties gaining employment shows the effects were uneven.
questions.hint: Hold all four figures in the report at once.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how rising operating costs feed general inflation and what a board controls
questions.stem: A transit board asks you to explain how rising transit costs feed into general inflation, and what the board can actually influence. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: When fuel, power, and vehicle costs rise, operators pass part of the increase to riders, and that higher cost of moving goods and people shows up in the prices shops charge, so a cost increase in one sector can spread through the economy as a general rise in prices. The board cannot set the price of energy, but it can limit how much of its own cost it passes on, and it can reduce fuel use through better routing, more efficient vehicles, and fewer empty miles.

questions.explanation: A strong answer traces the pass-through from operating costs to general prices and then identifies the levers the board actually controls. It should be clear about the limits of what any single agency can do.
questions.hint: Trace the pass-through, then list your own levers.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether two access measures address different bottlenecks
questions.stem: A transit board pairs a recruiting preference with scholarships at a local community college. Which combined judgment about the two is most accurate?

options.text: Both programs are redundant, since the local labor market already supplies enough
options.misconception: Assumes the current supply of workers is already sufficient

options.text: The scholarships make the preference unnecessary, since both serve the same applicants
options.misconception: Treats two different bottlenecks as one problem

options.text: The preference is ineffective without the scholarships, because applicants cannot qualify alone
options.misconception: Makes one measure depend entirely on the other

options.text: The preference opens current jobs and the scholarships widen the future pool, so they address different bottlenecks

questions.explanation: A preference changes who can win jobs that exist now, while scholarships build the qualified pool for later openings, so they address separate constraints. Either alone leaves a bottleneck.
questions.hint: Ask whether each measure works now or later.
